# A Cluster-Randomised Trial of a 30-Hour Week in Municipal Administration: Nine-Month Results

*Varden County Evaluation Unit, in collaboration with the Department of Labour Economics, Easterly University. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony and D. Rao. Registered protocol VC-2023-04.*

## Summary

We randomly assigned 24 administrative offices of a county government, employing 1,180 staff, to either reduce scheduled hours from 37.5 to 30 per week at full pay (12 offices) or continue on the standard schedule (12 offices) for nine months. Output was measured from administrative records, not from manager assessments, and actual hours from timesheets. The effect differed sharply by type of work. In case-processing offices, where work arrives as a backlog that can be cleared at any time, output per full-time employee changed by −2.1% (95% CI −6.8 to +2.6) relative to control and output per actual hour rose by 12.5%. In counter and contact-centre offices, where output depends on staff being present while the public is waiting, output per employee fell by 11.4% (95% CI −16.9 to −5.9), waiting times rose, and output per actual hour rose by a more modest 6.7%. Sick days fell by 29% across treated offices. An exploratory analysis suggests that a reduction in recurring meetings may account for part of the gain in case-processing offices.

## Motivation

Existing evidence on reduced working time comes mainly from voluntary pilots without comparison groups, in which output is often reported by the managers who sponsored the change. The county wished to know whether a reduced schedule could be extended to its own administrative staff without loss of service, and agreed to a randomised design with administrative output measures and a registered analysis plan.

## Design

**Units and randomisation.** The 24 offices were stratified into two strata by type of work before randomisation, and offices were randomised within strata:

- *Case-processing offices* (14 offices; 7 treated, 7 control): permits, licensing, benefits assessment and records. Work arrives as cases that join a queue and can be completed at any point within statutory deadlines.
- *Counter and contact-centre offices* (10 offices; 5 treated, 5 control): in-person service counters and telephone lines. Work arrives as members of the public who must be served while they wait.

Randomisation was at office level to avoid contamination between colleagues. Treated offices kept their public opening hours unchanged; staff rotas were rearranged so that each employee worked 30 scheduled hours.

**Outcomes.** The registered primary outcome is output per full-time-equivalent employee (FTE), measured as cases closed (case-processing) or contacts handled (counter and contact centre), from the county's case-management and telephony systems. Registered secondary outcomes are output per actual hour (from timesheets, which include any overtime claimed), quality (the share of decisions overturned on appeal; for contact centres, the repeat-contact rate within seven days), average waiting time, and sick days. Analysis is difference-in-differences against the six-month pre-period, with standard errors clustered by office.

**Exploratory measures.** At the request of office managers we also collected calendar data on recurring meetings in month six. This was not part of the registered plan.

## Results

### Hours

Scheduled hours fell by 20% in treated offices. Actual hours, from timesheets, fell by less: by 13% in case-processing offices (from 37.9 to 33.0 per week) and by 17% in counter offices (from 37.6 to 31.2), the difference reflecting overtime claimed to clear backlogs in case-processing. Control offices' actual hours were stable.

### Output and quality

**Table 1. Difference-in-differences estimates at nine months, treated relative to control**

| Outcome | Case-processing (7 v 7 offices) | Counter and contact centre (5 v 5 offices) |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −11.4% (−16.9 to −5.9) |
| Actual hours per FTE | −13% | −17% |
| Output per actual hour | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +6.7% (+0.4 to +13.3) |
| Appeal overturn rate / repeat contact rate | 3.1% v 3.0% | 11.8% v 10.9% |
| Average wait (minutes), treated offices, pre → month 9 | — | 4.2 → 6.9 |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% (both strata pooled) | |

In case-processing offices, output per employee was statistically indistinguishable from control, with a point estimate slightly below zero, and quality was unchanged. Because actual hours fell by 13%, output per actual hour rose by 12.5%. Measured against scheduled rather than actual hours, the gain would appear as 22%; we regard that figure as misleading, because staff did not in fact work only the scheduled hours.

In counter and contact-centre offices, the picture is different. With the same number of staff each working fewer hours, fewer staff were present at any given time during unchanged opening hours. Contacts handled per employee fell by 11.4% and the average wait rose from 4.2 to 6.9 minutes. Output per actual hour rose by 6.7%, but this did not offset the loss of hours, and the service the public received was worse. Abandoned calls rose from 6% to 10% of calls.

### Wellbeing

Sick days fell by 29% in treated offices relative to control. Resignations were lower in treated offices (annualised 3.9% against 7.4%), though with 12 offices per arm and few resignations the estimate is imprecise.

### Exploratory: meetings

Calendar data in month six showed that staff in treated case-processing offices spent 3.8 hours per week in recurring meetings against 7.1 hours in control case-processing offices, a difference of 3.3 hours. Offices that cut meetings most showed the largest gains in output per hour (correlation across the 7 treated offices, r = 0.71). Interviews suggested that the reduced schedule prompted managers to cancel standing meetings that had persisted by habit.

We emphasise that this analysis was not registered, that it rests on seven offices, and that a correlation across seven offices cannot establish a mechanism. We report it because, if confirmed, it would mean that a substantial part of the per-hour gain comes from removing low-value time rather than from rest alone, and that would matter for how the result is interpreted and for what other employers could expect. We have registered a confirmatory test for the 24-month follow-up.

## Discussion

Three conclusions follow from the registered analyses.

First, in work where output is not tied to presence, a 20% cut in scheduled hours produced a much smaller cut in actual hours and little or no measurable loss of output per employee. Output per hour rose by about an eighth.

Second, in work where output is tied to presence, the same change reduced output per employee by about a tenth and worsened service, even though each hour worked was somewhat more productive. Gains per hour do not by themselves imply that the hours reduction pays for itself. The question "does a shorter week raise productivity?" therefore has at least two answers depending on whether productivity is understood per hour or per employee, and these come apart most sharply in coverage-bound work.

Third, estimates computed against scheduled hours materially overstate the per-hour gain. In our data the overstatement is from 12.5% to 22% in case-processing offices.

These findings qualify claims, made on the basis of uncontrolled pilots, that reduced hours are sector-general. A sector may contain both kinds of work; what matters is whether output in a given role depends on hours of presence.

## Limitations

The trial is in one public employer, with 24 offices; confidence intervals are correspondingly wide, particularly in the counter stratum. Staff knew their assignment, and control staff knew that a trial was under way, which could have affected effort in either direction. Nine months may be too short to reveal whether gains persist after the novelty of the change wears off, or whether backlogs build up beyond the statutory deadlines. Public-sector case processing may differ from private-sector knowledge work in ways that affect the result. A 24-month follow-up is under way.

# A Critical Reading of the Varden County 30-Hour Trial (VC-2023-04)

This is a much stronger study than the Halden pilot, and it fixes most of the problems I raised there:

- **Randomised control group.** Offices were randomly assigned to the shorter week or the standard one.
- **Administrative output data.** Output comes from case and telephony records, not manager ratings.
- **Timesheet hours.** Productivity is measured against hours actually worked, not hours scheduled.
- **Registered analysis plan,** with the exploratory meeting analysis clearly labelled as such.
- **Stratification by the right variable:** whether output depends on staff being present.

The arithmetic checks out:

| Calculation | Result | Reported |
|---|---|---|
| Case-processing: 0.979 ÷ 0.87 | 1.125 | +12.5% ✓ |
| Counter: 0.886 ÷ 0.83 | 1.067 | +6.7% ✓ |
| Case-processing against scheduled hours: 0.979 ÷ 0.8 | 1.224 | 22% ✓ |
| Case-processing hours: 37.9 → 33.0 | −12.9% | −13% ✓ |
| Counter hours: 37.6 → 31.2 | −17.0% | −17% ✓ |

The conclusions are also appropriately hedged. Even so, there are real gaps.

## 1. Cost is never measured, and overtime may reverse the case-processing result

Timesheets "include any overtime claimed." In case-processing offices, actual hours were about 33 against a schedule of 30, roughly 3 hours a week above schedule. If that time was paid as overtime on top of full salary, possibly at a premium rate:

- labour cost per employee rose by perhaps 8–12%,
- while output per employee fell by about 2%,
- so cost per case closed rose by roughly a tenth.

That would turn the "success" stratum into a cost increase. It is the opposite of the Halden bargain of full pay for full output.

The paper never says whether overtime was paid in cash, taken as time off in lieu, or unpaid. It never reports cost per case. For a county that wants to know whether this can be extended "without loss of service", cost per unit of output is the key number.

There is a second, opposite risk. Timesheets record only overtime that was *claimed*. Unclaimed work, such as reading email at home, would make the true reduction in hours smaller and the per-hour gain smaller still.

## 2. Waiting times, abandoned calls and quality are not analysed as difference-in-differences

The registered method compares treated offices with controls, before and after. Several outcomes are reported without that comparison:

- **Waiting time (4.2 → 6.9 minutes)** and **abandoned calls (6% → 10%)** are treated offices only, before and after. No control trend is shown. If control waits also rose, perhaps through seasonal demand, the treatment effect is overstated.
- **Quality** is shown as treated against control levels (3.1% v 3.0%; 11.8% v 10.9%). There is no pre-period and no confidence interval.
- **The repeat-contact rise** in counter offices (+0.9 points) is never discussed.
- **"Quality was unchanged"** in case-processing is an assertion. The data shown cannot support it without an interval.

## 3. With so few offices, the confidence intervals are probably too narrow

Standard errors are clustered by office, but there are only 14 clusters in one stratum and 10 in the other. Conventional cluster-robust errors are known to be anti-conservative at these sizes. The paper should report wild-cluster bootstrap or randomisation-inference p-values.

This matters most for the counter stratum's per-hour gain (+0.4 to +13.3). Its lower bound barely clears zero and may not survive a small-sample correction. The authors call the counter intervals wide, but they may be wider still.

## 4. Case-processing backlog and case mix are unmeasured

- **The backlog may be growing.** If cases arrive at a steady rate and closures per employee fell by about 2%, the queue is getting longer. The limitations section acknowledges this, but nine months of data could already show it. Backlog size and time to decision should be reported.
- **Case mix may have shifted.** Under time pressure, staff can close easy cases first. Counts of cases closed would then flatter productivity while hard cases age. Time-to-decision, or a breakdown by complexity, would rule this out.
- **The interval cannot rule out a loss.** "Statistically indistinguishable from control" is not the same as no loss. The interval (−6.8% to +2.6%) is consistent with a meaningful decline.

## 5. The sick-day figure has the same mechanical problem as Halden

The paper doesn't say whether the 30 hours were worked as four days or as five shorter days. If staff work fewer days, there are fewer days on which anyone can report sick, and part of the 29% fall follows automatically.

Sick days should be expressed per scheduled working day, and broken out by stratum. The pooled figure also has no confidence interval. Resignations are rightly flagged as imprecise.

## 6. The meetings analysis is properly caveated but has one more gap

The authors are admirably careful here, and they have registered a confirmatory test. A few further points:

- **No baseline.** Calendar data were collected only in month six, so the 3.3-hour difference is a single snapshot comparison, not a before-and-after change. With seven offices per arm, chance imbalance at baseline is plausible.
- **The correlation is very uncertain.** With r = 0.71 across seven offices, the 95% interval runs roughly from zero to 0.95.
- **Counter offices are missing.** Meeting data for that stratum are not reported.
- **The scale invites a further question.** Removing 3.3 hours of meetings accounts for a large share of the roughly 5-hour fall in actual hours. If the result is confirmed, it suggests some of the benefit is available without cutting hours at all. A meetings-only arm would test this.

## 7. Counter offices: the trial tested one option, not the policy

Treated counter offices kept the same staff and the same opening hours, so fewer people were on duty at any time. That outcome was predictable. The more useful policy question is how many extra staff would be needed to restore service, and at what cost.

With a +6.7% per-hour gain, restoring output needs about 11% more paid hours than the reduced schedule provides. A simple costing would show whether that is affordable.

## 8. Generalisability and awareness of assignment

- **One public employer.** Public offices have no profit motive and have statutory deadlines that act as a backstop. The authors acknowledge this.
- **Control staff may have been discouraged.** Control staff knew the trial existed. Resentment could lower their effort or raise their resignations (7.4%, against 3.9% in treated offices). That would inflate the treatment effects, not just add noise in either direction.
- **"Output per FTE" is ambiguous.** It should be confirmed that FTE means headcount here. If 30 hours were counted as 0.8 FTE, the figures would mean something different.

## How it compares with the Halden pilot

The two studies fit together well, and this one explains why the Halden pilot misled:

| Point | Halden pilot | Varden trial |
|---|---|---|
| Per-hour gain against scheduled hours | +23% | about +22% in case-processing |
| Per-hour gain against actual hours | not measured | +12.5% case-processing, +6.7% counter |
| Customer-facing work | output fell 7%; half of retail organisations reverted | output per employee fell 11%; service worse |

Halden's headline gain is almost exactly what Varden gets by dividing by scheduled rather than actual hours. Correcting to actual hours roughly halves it. The randomised data also confirm the pattern visible in Halden's own continuation figures: work that depends on staff being present suffers.

## What the evidence supports

**Supported:**
- In backlog-type work, a shorter week cost little measurable output per employee over nine months.
- Output per actual hour rose by roughly 10–15%.
- Some of that gain plausibly came from cutting low-value meetings.

**Not supported:**
- That it is cost-neutral. This is unknown until overtime and cost per case are reported.
- That it works for counter and contact-centre work without extra staff. It does not.
- That the gains persist. Nine months is too short to tell.

The most useful additions would be:
1. cost per unit of output, including overtime;
2. difference-in-differences estimates for waiting times and quality;
3. small-sample-corrected confidence intervals;
4. backlog size and time-to-decision data.
